questions.question: What does `position: relative` on a parent establish for an `absolute`-positioned child?
options: Nothing — absolute positioning always ignores ancestors
It becomes the positioning context the child is positioned relative to, instead of the viewport or a further-up ancestor
It forces the child to stay in normal document flow
It disables z-index on the child
questions.explanation: An absolutely positioned element is positioned relative to its nearest non-static ancestor; relative is the most common way to deliberately create that anchor.

questions.question: Besides `fixed`/`sticky` positioning, what else can create a new stacking context?
questions.explanation: Several CSS properties beyond position create new stacking contexts, including opacity < 1, transform, and filter — all common culprits in unexpected z-index behavior.

questions.question: A child with `z-index: 9999` is trapped behind a sibling subtree with a lower z-index. What's the most likely cause?
options: 9999 is too large a number for browsers to handle
An ancestor of the child has created its own stacking context (e.g. via opacity or transform), so the child's z-index only competes within that ancestor, not globally
z-index only works on absolutely positioned elements
questions.explanation: Once an ancestor forms a stacking context, its own z-index value (not any descendant's) is what competes with sibling stacking contexts — descendants can't escape to compete globally.

questions.question: What happens to an element with `position: absolute` if no ancestor has a non-static position?
options: It is removed from the page entirely
It positions itself relative to the initial containing block, effectively the viewport
It throws a CSS error and is ignored
It falls back to position: static
questions.explanation: Without any positioned ancestor, an absolutely positioned element's containing block defaults to the root/viewport.
